newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lufthansa hardens stance on eve of pilots strike ballot.
newsitem.headline: Lufthansa hardens stance on eve of pilots strike ballot.

text.p: Lufthansa AG, hardening its stance a day before the results of a strike vote by pilots and flight attendants will be released, said Tuesday it would not change the pay offer the union has already rejected.

The German airline said the "overwhelming majority" of its 58,000 workers were against a walkout by pilots and flight attendants who are members of the DAG union. The airline added that "clearly less than 10 percent" of its work force was in the union.

Lufthansa said its offer of new talks with the DAG was still on the table but that it saw little room to manoeuvre from the deal it signed in October 1996 with the OeTV union that represents ground personnel at the airline.

The DAG union plans Wednesday to release the results of balloting that would give union leaders the right to call a strike. DAG members must give at least 70 percent approval, a level the union has said would be met.
The DAG has said a strike would only be called if attempts at talks with Lufthansa management were to fail but has said it would not return to talks unless a new offer was made.

"The current conflict is, among other things, being led by workers who are among the better wage-earners at the company but also work in an area where 170 new jobs were created last year," the airline said in a statement.
Pilots and flight attendants are opposed to the OeTV deal, which Lufthansa reached with the union after talks with the DAG broke off last autumn.

The 27-month contract agreed to by the OeTV calls for Lufthansa workers to receive a one-time payment equal to one-third of a month's base pay, a 1.7 percent raise in 1998 and a small bonus in cash or Lufthansa stock.

The DAG has demanded a higher wage offer and wants only a one-year deal, the top priority for a union reluctant to get locked into a multiyear contract as the airline seeks to cut costs to improve its competitive stance when European skies are opened in April.
Lufthansa's statement was the latest effort to isolate DAG members, who staged two brief warning strikes in November and December that cost Lufthansa 30 million marks ($18 million).
Lufthansa has said the impact of a strike on its future could be "fatal."
